details:
**Snow Country**
Kawabata's most famous novel, set in a remote hot-spring town in Japan's snowy western mountains (the town is identified with Yuzawa). It follows a Tokyo visitor's doomed love affair with a local geisha. It was central to his 1968 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first won by a Japanese writer.

**Shimamura**
The idle, wealthy protagonist of Snow Country. He calls himself an expert on Western ballet and writes about it, even though he has never seen a ballet performed. Over several visits to the hot-spring town, he slowly realizes he cannot truly return Komako's love.

**Komako**
The passionate geisha in Snow Country who has an affair with Shimamura. She taught herself the shamisen by practicing alone and copying music broadcasts. Shimamura notices the shift in their relationship when he starts calling her a "good woman" instead of a "good girl."

**The Master of Go**
Kawabata's semi-fictional novel based on his own newspaper reporting of the 1938 "retirement game" of Go. The match, played on a 19-by-19 board, lasted about six months and pitted the aging master against a younger challenger. It is narrated by the reporter Uragami, Kawabata's stand-in.

**Milky Way and the warehouse fire**
The famous ending of Snow Country. A fire breaks out in a former silkworm-cocoon warehouse, and Yoko falls from the balcony while Komako rushes to carry her out. Shimamura stumbles and feels "the Milky Way flow down inside him with a roar." The novel never makes clear whether Yoko is dead or only unconscious.

**Thousand Cranes**
A novel built around the Japanese tea ceremony, in which the young Kikuji Mitani is drawn into the lives of his late father's mistresses. The title refers to the thousand-crane pattern on the kerchief (furoshiki) carried by Yukiko Inamura, a young woman proposed to Kikuji as a bride.

**Honinbo Shusai and Otake**
The opponents in The Master of Go. Shusai, the aging Meijin (Master), loses his retirement game to the young challenger Otake, a fictionalized version of the real player Minoru Kitani. Shusai dies about a year after the match.

**Sealed move (Black 121)**
The controversial move in The Master of Go. Otake sealed Black 121 at the end of a session, a tactical maneuver that outraged Shusai and seemed to violate the spirit of the game. The game ended with Black 237.

**Mrs. Ota and Kikuji**
In Thousand Cranes, Mrs. Ota, the mistress of Kikuji's late father, begins an affair with Kikuji and later kills herself, possibly with sleeping pills. Kikuji then becomes involved with her daughter Fumiko. Fumiko breaks a white Shino bowl stained with her mother's lipstick and then vanishes.

**The Sound of the Mountain**
A novel about the aging Shingo Ogata, who hears a rumbling from the mountain at night and takes it as an omen of death. He is troubled by his son Shuichi's affair with a war widow and by his own tender feelings for his daughter-in-law Kikuko. The novel ends with a proposal for a family trip to see the autumn maples.

**"The Dancing Girl of Izu"**
An early story about a student on a walking tour of the Izu Peninsula who falls for a young drum-carrying dancer in a troupe of traveling performers. When he sees her run naked from a public bath and wave to him, he realizes she is "a mere child" and laughs with relief.

**Yoko**
The second woman of Snow Country. Shimamura first sees her eye floating in the train window as a reflection, while she tends to the ailing Yukio, the son of Komako's music teacher. Her "beautiful, almost sad" voice haunts Shimamura until she falls in the warehouse fire.

**Palm-of-the-Hand Stories**
Kawabata's collection of very short stories written over his whole career. It includes "The Grasshopper and the Bell Cricket," in which children hunt insects with homemade paper lanterns, and "The Pomegranate," in which Kimiko holds onto the fruit her brother touched before leaving for war. Kawabata also condensed Snow Country into one of these stories.

**Chikako Kurimoto**
A tea ceremony teacher in Thousand Cranes and a former mistress of Kikuji's father. She has a large black birthmark on her breast, an image that haunts Kikuji. She meddles in his life by pushing his marriage to Yukiko Inamura.

**The House of the Sleeping Beauties**
A novella in which Old Eguchi repeatedly visits a secret inn. There, elderly men pay to spend the night beside drugged, naked young women who never wake. The book is a meditation on age, memory, and desire.
